solar-22.quote: In the event that a load drawn from the battery exceeds the charge current, the charge controller will no longer be able to maintain the battery to a Float set point and the charge controller will end the float charging stage and refer back to bulk charging.
solar-22.doc_title: Renogy Rover Li Series MPPT Solar Charge Controller User Manual
solar-22.section: Charging and Activation Logic - Float Charging

solar-23.claim: Terminal battery voltage includes an IR drop that depends on load current, the battery's internal impedance and battery temperature. Load and charge currents and battery temperature are therefore physical parents of battery voltage.
solar-23.relation: mppt_load_current, mppt_battery_charge_current, mppt_battery_temperature -> mppt_battery_voltage (physical, IR drop)
solar-23.quote: Voltage + IR Correction expands on voltage correlation by taking into account the IR drop that occurs when a load is applied to a battery. The amount of IR drop depends on the internal impedance of the battery, the amount of load current, and the temperature of the battery.
solar-23.doc_title: TI SLUAAR3 Battery Gauging Algorithm Comparison

solar-24.claim: MPPT charging only works when the PV voltage is at least about 2 V above the battery voltage. At dawn, dusk and night the charge current is 0 even with some light.

solar-25.claim: PV current falls with less light, and PV open-circuit voltage falls with higher panel temperature. light_lux is a physical parent of solar current only if the light sensor sees the same irradiance as the panel (placement unknown). Panel temperature is not a node, and enclosure_temperature is not panel temperature.
solar-25.relation: light_lux -> mppt_solar_current (physical, proxy); panel temperature (unobserved) -> mppt_solar_voltage
solar-25.quote: Current decreases with dwindling light ... Open-circuit voltage decreases with rising temperature
solar-25.doc_title: SRNE ML4860 Solar Charge and Discharge Controller User Manual
solar-25.section: Fig. 1-2 Solar panel output characteristic curve (figure annotations)

solar-26.claim: Higher ambient temperature lowers the panel's Vmp and limits generation. This supports a weak ambient-temperature effect on PV voltage, through panel temperature, which is not observed.
solar-26.relation: panel temperature (unobserved) -> mppt_solar_voltage; enclosure_temperature only a weak proxy
solar-26.quote: High temperature is the natural enemy of solar panels. With the increase of ambient temperature, the operating voltage (Vmp) of the solar panel decreases, which limits the power generation of the solar panel.
solar-26.doc_title: Renogy Rover Li Series MPPT Solar Charge Controller User Manual

solar-27.claim: The PV voltage at the controller input is about 0 at night, so time of day (sun) is a parent of solar voltage and current. This is the dataset authors' reading.
solar-27.quote: Solar-panel voltage at the controller input (about 0 at night). *Source: `sqlite:mppt`.*
solar-27.section: Battery and solar charge controller (MPPT), device_mppt_solar_voltage

solar-28.claim: The battery temperature is measured by an external probe stuck to the battery surface (the Rover protocol calls it the battery's surface temperature). It is a battery-surface reading, not the controller's or the enclosure's temperature.
solar-28.quote: Adhere the sensor on the top or side of the battery with the insulation tape.
solar-28.doc_title: Renogy Rover Li Series MPPT Solar Charge Controller User Manual

solar-29.claim: Against physical edges into battery temperature: on SRNE controllers without a probe, the battery temperature reads a constant default of 25 °C, so it carries no physical information on such devices.
solar-29.quote: If no temperature sensor is connected to the controller, the battery temperature value will stay at a default of 25 °C.
solar-29.doc_title: SRNE ML4860 Solar Charge and Discharge Controller User Manual

solar-30.claim: Temperature compensation: the battery temperature probe adjusts the charging voltage set points (-3 mV/°C/2V for lead-acid; 0 for lithium, no compensation). Battery temperature is then a control parent of battery voltage during absorption and float, but only for non-lithium chemistries.
solar-30.quote: Temperature Compensation Non-lithium: -3mV / °C / 2V Lithium: 0mV / °C / 2V; no compensation
solar-30.doc_title: Renogy Rover Li Series MPPT Solar Charge Controller User Manual

solar-31.claim: Battery temperature protection: below a low-temperature threshold (default 0 °C for lithium) or above 65 °C, the controller stops charging and discharging. In cold weather, battery temperature can force the charge current and the load to 0.
solar-31.relation: mppt_battery_temperature -> mppt_battery_charge_current (control: cutoff below LTPT / above 65 C)
solar-31.quote: When the temperature detected by the optional temperature sensor is lower than the Low-Temperature Protection Threshold(LTPT), the controller will stop charging and discharging automatically.
solar-31.section: 4.1 Protection (9 Lithium battery low temperature protection)

solar-32.claim: Temperatures use sign-magnitude encoding: 0x800A means -10 °C, and the table says 'b7: sign bit'. The README's 129-131 °C battery readings (0x81-0x83) and 32770-32773 minimum readings (0x8002-0x8005) are probably sub-zero temperatures decoded without the sign bit, not sensor faults. This is an inference.
solar-32.quote: Parsing: 0020H indicates the battery's surface temperature is 30 °C, and if the figure turns out to be 800AH, then it indicates the battery's surface temperature is -10 °C
solar-32.section: 3.7 To read the battery's surface temperature and controller temperature

solar-33.claim: SOC estimation, Renogy Rover: the controller's SOC is estimated from battery (charging) voltage, not coulomb counting. mppt_battery_soc_pct is then a derived function of mppt_battery_voltage, not an independent measurement.
solar-33.quote: The Battery Capacity (SOC%) is estimated based on the charging voltage.

solar-34.claim: The SRNE protocol defines SOC only as 'current battery capacity value' and does not give the method. Its SOC-based end-of-charge and end-of-discharge parameters are marked 'Unrealized', so SRNE firmware probably does not use SOC for control.
solar-34.quote: 8 higher bits: end-of-charge SOC E00FH 2 R/W - Unrealized 8 lower bits: end-of-discharge SOC

solar-35.claim: EPEVER defines SOC as the percentage of remaining capacity and has a 'voltage compensation vs SOC' management mode, but does not give the algorithm.
solar-35.quote: Battery SOC 311A 04（read） The percentage of battery's remaining capacity % 1

solar-36.claim: A voltage-correlation SOC is not corrected for current, temperature or battery age, and is accurate only at rest. While charging or under load, it is biased by the charge and load currents and by temperature, through battery voltage. This is a reason to route those effects through battery voltage rather than add direct edges.
solar-36.relation: mppt_battery_voltage -> mppt_battery_soc_pct; currents/temperature act only via voltage
solar-36.quote: Also, SOC is not adjusted for important factors like discharge rate, temperature, and the age of the battery. Because of this factor, we recommend using voltage correlation for applications where the battery has long periods of rest
solar-36.doc_title: TI SLUAAR3 Battery Gauging Algorithm Comparison

solar-37.claim: The controller draws its own small supply current (static losses ≤8 mA at 12 V on EPEVER; ≤100 mA at 12 V on Rover). This is an unobserved battery drain and a small heat source, too small to need a node.

solar-38.claim: The README describes the sign's input voltage as 'battery / supply'. On solar devices the INA238 input is probably fed from the battery, either through the controller's load output or directly. If it is on the load output, input_voltage ≈ mppt_load_voltage, input_current ≈ mppt_load_current and input_power ≈ mppt_load_power (redundancy). This is not confirmed.
solar-38.relation: candidate redundancy (unconfirmed): mppt_load_voltage ~ input_voltage_volts; mppt_load_current ~ input_current_amperes; mppt_load_power ~ input_power_watts
solar-38.quote: Voltage at the device's power input (battery / supply). *Source: `sysfs:ina238`.*

solar-39.claim: All MPPT meanings in the dataset are the dataset authors' reading of names and data, not vendor documentation. Every README-based MPPT relation above is inferred.
solar-39.quote: The endpoint's `# HELP` only repeats the metric name, so **units, meanings and notes are our reading of the names and of the data, not vendor documentation**.

readme-1.claim: Every unit, meaning and note in the README is the dataset authors' reading of metric names and data, not vendor documentation. Each README-based edge below therefore rests on an inferred meaning, and the README's 'typical' ranges are data summaries that must not be used to set edges.
readme-1.quote: The endpoint's `# HELP` only repeats the metric name, so **units, meanings and notes are our reading of the names and of the data, not vendor documentation**.

readme-2.claim: Source tags separate direct hardware reads (sysfs:*) from values that a service wrote to its local sqlite database (sqlite:<service>) and from values computed on the device (calc:*). So heartbeat metrics such as cpu_gpu_power and device_power travel a different software path, with possibly different timing, than the sysfs INA238/INA3221/thermal metrics.
readme-2.relation: none (provenance: sysfs vs sqlite:heartbeat vs calc)
readme-2.quote: (`sysfs:*` = Linux hardware sensors, `sqlite:<service>` = the device's local database written by that service, `calc:*` = computed on the device, `proc:` / `log:` / `cmd:` = process, log or systemd checks)

readme-3.claim: The README describes input power as approximately input voltage times input current and gives the same chip (INA238) as the source of all three. This makes P = V x I an identity edge at the sample level; 'about' leaves room for conversion timing or rounding.
readme-3.relation: input_power_watts = input_voltage_volts x input_current_amperes (identity, per sample, one INA238)
readme-3.quote: Power drawn at the device's input (about input voltage x input current). *Source: `sysfs:ina238`.*
readme-3.section: Power and energy table, row device_input_power_watts

readme-4.claim: Input current also comes from the INA238 and is defined at the same power input as voltage and power, so V, I and P are three readings of one sensor at one point (a shared-cause / identity triple). The README does not say which loads sit behind that input.
readme-4.relation: input_current_amperes, input_voltage_volts, input_power_watts share one sensor (INA238) at one point
readme-4.quote: Current drawn at the device's power input. *Source: `sysfs:ina238`.*
readme-4.section: Power and energy table, row device_input_current_amperes

readme-5.claim: Input voltage is the 'battery / supply' voltage, and some devices run near 55.9 V instead of 11-14 V. The supply type therefore sets the voltage level, and through I = P/V it sets the current level for a given power. The README counts about 11 such devices; the task brief says 13.
readme-5.relation: supply_56v -> input_voltage_volts (sets nominal level); input_current_amperes = input_power_watts / input_voltage_volts
readme-5.quote: Voltage at the device's power input (battery / supply). *Source: `sysfs:ina238`.* **Note:** Most devices read about 11-14 V, but about 11 devices run at about 55.9 V (roughly 12% of all samples are above 20 V), so do not assume a 12 V system.
readme-5.section: Power and energy table, row device_input_voltage_volts

readme-6.claim: Textbook physics gives electric power as current times voltage. This supports the identity form for the INA238 triple and also for the MPPT load, charge and solar triples, which the README never states explicitly.
readme-6.relation: P = V x I (identity) for each co-located V/I/P triple
readme-6.quote: The power supplied from the battery is equal to current times the voltage, P=IV.
readme-6.doc_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 2, 9.5 Electrical Energy and Power

readme-7.claim: The energy counter is computed on the device by integrating input power over time. Its hourly increase (input_energy_rate_w, Wh per hour) is therefore the time-average input power over the hour. The README does not say which power value is integrated (the INA238 power reading or V x I) or at what step.
readme-7.relation: input_energy_rate_w = time-mean of input power over the hour (identity, approximately equal to hourly mean of input_power_watts)
readme-7.quote: Energy used, computed on the device by integrating input power over time. *Source: `calc:integrated_input_power`.* **Note:** Falls back to 0 about once a day (see Notes on the data), so it is not a lifetime total.
readme-7.section: Power and energy table, row device_input_energy_wh_total

readme-8.claim: Average power is the energy delivered in an interval divided by the interval. So a Wh increase over exactly 1 h equals the time-average power in W, while the hourly gauge mean of input_power_watts is a mean of about 30 point samples taken 120 s apart. The two agree only as far as the point samples represent the time-average (sub-120 s bursts are missed by the gauge but included in the integral if the device integrates faster).
readme-8.relation: input_energy_rate_w (integral/1h) ~ mean(input_power_watts samples); residual from sampling
readme-8.quote: we first define average power as the work done during a time interval, divided by the interval

readme-9.claim: The counters reset to 0 repeatedly. Most drops fall in the 05:00 UTC hour, which the README reads as local midnight; the rest happen at device restarts. Energy consumed between the last sample before a restart and the restart is not in the counter, so input_energy_rate_w can undershoot mean input power in restart hours.
readme-9.relation: none (counter-reset caveat affecting input_energy_rate_w vs input_power_watts)
readme-9.quote: `input_energy_wh_total`, `pir_count`, `ds_consumer_error_total` and the `wwan_*_gb` values fall back to 0 repeatedly: about three quarters of those drops happen in the 05:00 UTC hour (they look like daily totals that restart at local midnight), the rest at device restarts.
readme-9.section: Notes on the data, 'Totals that reset'

readme-10.claim: features.py (project code) computes counter rates as the reset-aware increase from the previous stored sample of the same scrape target, whatever the time gap. A drop counts the new value as the increase, and the first sample counts 0. After a scrape gap of several hours, the whole gap's energy lands in the first hour after the gap, so input_energy_rate_w then exceeds that hour's mean input power. A reset inside a gap loses the pre-reset part.
readme-10.relation: input_energy_rate_w != mean(input_power_watts) in hours after gaps or resets (processing artefact)
readme-10.doc_title: analysis/features.py: hourly feature builder (project code, not documentation)

readme-11.claim: The counter rate is the increase per bucket, and the bucket defaults to one hour. input_energy_rate_w equals mean watts only with --freq h; with 30min buckets it would be Wh per 30 min (half the mean power). Increases are credited to the bucket of the later sample, which shifts the window by up to one sample interval.
readme-11.relation: input_energy_rate_w [Wh/bucket] = mean W only when bucket = 1 h
readme-11.quote: * counters (running totals that reset daily) -> hourly increase, reset-aware (`*_rate`)
readme-11.doc_title: analysis/features.py: hourly feature builder (project code, not documentation)

readme-12.claim: Gauges and binary metrics become the hourly mean of clean samples, and each metric is aggregated separately. A sample-level product identity therefore becomes mean(P) = mean(V) x mean(I) + within-hour cov(V, I) at the hourly level, not an exact product. Linear identities (sums, differences, containment as a sum of parts) commute with the mean only if every term is averaged over the same sample instants.
readme-12.relation: hourly: mean(P) = mean(V) x mean(I) + cov_hour(V,I)
readme-12.quote: * gauges / binary metrics -> hourly mean of clean samples (placeholder codes excluded)
readme-12.doc_title: analysis/features.py: hourly feature builder (project code, not documentation)

readme-13.claim: The covariance shortcut formula gives the size of the hourly product-identity residual: the mean of a product equals the product of the means plus the covariance. The residual is zero only if V or I is constant within the hour (e.g. a stiff 12 V or 56 V supply). It is non-zero when voltage moves within the hour, as it would on battery or charge-controlled devices.
readme-13.quote: The covariance can also be computed as: Cov[X, Y] = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]
readme-13.doc_title: Dennis Sun, Introduction to Probability, Lesson 29 Covariance

readme-14.claim: Metrics of one scrape are read within a few ms of each other, so the INA238 V, I and P samples are near-simultaneous and the sample-level identity is tight. However, metrics are not guaranteed to share timestamps or sample counts, and features.py drops the per-metric counts. An hourly V, I or P mean can thus cover different sample sets, a further source of identity residual that the detector cannot see.
readme-14.relation: identity residual also from unmatched sample sets per hour
readme-14.quote: Device metrics are stamped with the device's own reading time (metrics of one scrape are a few ms apart);

readme-15.claim: The README warns that metrics are scraped at different intervals and timestamps need not align across metrics. This weakens any lag-0 identity between metrics from different sources (sysfs vs sqlite:heartbeat vs sqlite:mppt) more than between metrics of one INA238.
readme-15.relation: cross-source relations are approximate within an hour
readme-15.quote: Metrics are scraped at different intervals; do not assume timestamps align across metrics.

readme-16.claim: device_power (heartbeat) has no documented definition, and the README says outright that it is not the same as input power. This argues AGAINST an identity edge device_power_watts = input_power_watts. Any edge into device_power_watts would be a guess until BusPas defines it.
readme-16.quote: Device power as recorded by the heartbeat service. *Source: `sqlite:heartbeat`.* **Note:** Not the same as `input_power_watts` (median about 5 W vs about 10 W); its exact definition is not documented.
readme-16.section: Power and energy table, row device_power

readme-17.claim: cpu_gpu_power is CPU + GPU power as logged by the heartbeat service into sqlite; the README names no sensor or rail. A containment edge into orin_power_watts (CPU+GPU rail as part of module power) is plausible but not documented here.
readme-17.relation: cpu_gpu_power_watts contained in orin_power_watts (inferred, sensor undocumented)
readme-17.quote: CPU + GPU power draw, as logged by the heartbeat service. *Source: `sqlite:heartbeat`.*
readme-17.section: Power and energy table, row device_cpu_gpu_power_watts

readme-18.claim: orin_power is the Jetson Orin module's power from the INA3221 rail monitor, a different chip from the INA238 that measures input power. The relation to input power can only be containment (the module is one load among others), not identity. The README does not say that the module is downstream of the INA238 shunt, or which INA3221 channel is read.
readme-18.relation: orin_power_watts contained in input_power_watts (inferred; topology undocumented)
readme-18.quote: Power drawn by the Jetson Orin compute module (rail monitor). *Source: `sysfs:ina3221`.*
readme-18.section: Power and energy table, row device_orin_power_watts

readme-19.claim: board_temp is read from the INA238 power monitor, the same chip as input V/I/P, so it is that chip's own temperature sensor. The README's label 'board temperature' is its interpretation; how far the chip sits from heat sources is undocumented.
readme-19.relation: board_temp_celsius = INA238 die temperature (same chip as input_*); heating paths need other sources
readme-19.quote: Board temperature, read from the INA238 power-monitor chip. *Source: `sysfs:ina238`.*

readme-20.claim: CPU and GPU temperatures both come from Linux thermal sysfs. The README says nothing about their placement or coupling, so any redundancy or heating edge needs NVIDIA documentation. features.py drops GPU values <= -200 (the -256 error code) but applies no filter to CPU temperature.
readme-20.quote: GPU temperature. *Source: `sysfs:thermal`.* **Note:** One device reports exactly -256 about 30,000 times: a sensor error value, not a temperature.

readme-21.claim: Textbook physics: electrical power dissipated in a resistive element becomes heat. This is the generic mechanism behind power-to-temperature physical edges (e.g. CPU/GPU power heating CPU/GPU sensors, converter losses heating the board or controller). Specific thermal paths and delays need NVIDIA, TI or charge-controller documents.
readme-21.relation: dissipated power heats nearby sensors (generic physical mechanism)
readme-21.quote: With a resistor, the voltage drop across the resistor is dissipated as heat.
readme-21.doc_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 2, 9.5 Electrical Energy and Power

readme-22.claim: battery_soc_pct comes from the on-device power manager (sqlite:powermanager). It covers about 40 devices, while MPPT SoC covers about 17 and only about 13 have the MPPT. The README does not say that both measure the same battery, so a redundancy edge mppt_battery_soc_pct -> battery_soc_pct is inferred. features.py drops values above 100.
readme-22.relation: battery_soc_pct ~ mppt_battery_soc_pct (redundancy, inferred; same battery unconfirmed)
readme-22.quote: Battery state of charge as reported by the on-device power manager. *Source: `sqlite:powermanager`.* **Note:** A few readings above 100 (up to 113) are errors.
readme-22.section: Battery and solar charge controller table, row device_battery_remaining_capacity

readme-23.claim: The charge controller exposes SoC under two names that are meant to be identical, yet the README notes they usually differ. This argues against treating even a documented duplicate SoC as an exact redundancy, and suggests a loose tolerance for any SoC redundancy edge.
readme-23.relation: against exact redundancy between SoC readings
readme-23.quote: The two are meant to be identical. *Source: `sqlite:mppt`.* **Note:** In the data the two usually differ: on the 14 devices that report both, they agree within 0.5 points in only about 19% of paired samples
readme-23.section: Battery and solar charge controller table, row device_mppt_battery_remaining_capacity_mppt

readme-24.claim: The device itself estimates SoC from input voltage with a polynomial, so BusPas treats input voltage as battery voltage on at least some devices. The README calls this estimate rough and gives an example where it was far off, which argues AGAINST a strong input_voltage_volts -> battery SoC edge.
readme-24.quote: Battery state of charge estimated on the device from the input voltage with a 5th-degree polynomial. *Source: `calc:poly5`.* **Note:** A rough estimate, not a measurement: in a live sample it read 1.2 % while the battery reported 76.75 %.
readme-24.section: Battery and solar charge controller table, row device_input_soc_poly5_percent

readme-25.claim: The README defines load voltage, current and power as quantities on the controller's load output, but does not say that load power equals load voltage times load current; that identity rests on physics (P = IV). The README also does not say that the load output feeds the sign's INA238 input.
readme-25.relation: mppt_load_power = mppt_load_voltage x mppt_load_current (physics); mppt_load_power -> input_power_watts only if wired in series (unconfirmed)
readme-25.quote: Power drawn by the load on the controller's load output. *Source: `sqlite:mppt`.*
readme-25.section: Battery and solar charge controller table, rows device_mppt_load_current / _load_power / _load_voltage

readme-26.claim: Charge power is the power the controller delivers into the battery, and charge current is the current into the battery from the controller. Physics then gives charge power = battery voltage x charge current, though the README does not state it. Whether charge current is net of load current is undefined.
readme-26.relation: mppt_charge_power = mppt_battery_voltage x mppt_battery_charge_current (physics, not README-stated)
readme-26.quote: Power the charge controller delivers into the battery (0 at night). *Source: `sqlite:mppt`.*
readme-26.section: Battery and solar charge controller table, rows device_mppt_charge_power / _battery_charge_current / _battery_voltage

readme-27.claim: Solar voltage and current are measured at the controller input and are about 0 at night. Solar input power (not a node) = solar V x I, and charge power can be at most that, minus converter losses (energy conservation). The README gives no efficiency figure, so that must come from the controller vendor. Daylight (time_of_day, or light_lux if the light sensor sees the same sky as the panel, which is undocumented) is the physical driver.
readme-27.relation: mppt_charge_power <= mppt_solar_voltage x mppt_solar_current; time_of_day -> mppt_solar_current
readme-27.quote: Current from the solar panel into the controller (0 at night). *Source: `sqlite:mppt`.*
readme-27.section: Battery and solar charge controller table, rows device_mppt_solar_current / _solar_voltage

readme-28.claim: Load state reports whether the controller's load output is on. When it is off, load current and load power on that output must be 0 (a control gate). Hourly, the mean of a 0/1 flag is the fraction of samples on, so the gate becomes a product: mean(load_current) = mean(state) x mean(current | on) plus a covariance term.
readme-28.quote: Whether the controller's load output is on (1) or off (0). *Source: `sqlite:mppt`.*
readme-28.section: Battery and solar charge controller table, row device_mppt_load_state

readme-29.claim: The mppt_* metrics exist only on devices with a solar charge controller, so has_solar is a structural gate: MPPT nodes are defined only when has_solar = 1. The README does not define how has_solar or supply_56v are built (features.py does not build them).
readme-29.relation: has_solar -> existence of mppt_* nodes (context gate)
readme-29.quote: for example the `mppt_*` metrics exist only on devices with a solar charge controller, and humidity / light / temperature on a subset.
readme-29.section: Notes on the data, 'Not every device reports every metric'

readme-30.claim: features.py excludes placeholder values only for some MPPT fields (charge current, battery voltage and solar voltage equal to 100; battery temperature >= 120). It has no filter for load_*, charge_power, solar_current or controller temperature. Unfiltered placeholder codes in those fields would look like identity violations to the detector.
readme-30.doc_title: analysis/features.py: hourly feature builder (project code, not documentation)

readme-31.claim: Battery temperature comes from the charge controller's sensor, and controller temperature from the controller itself. The README documents no relation between them or to enclosure temperature; known 129-131 C fault values are filtered in features.py (>= 120).
readme-31.quote: Battery temperature from the charge controller's sensor. *Source: `sqlite:mppt`.* **Note:** About 1,500 samples read 129-131 °C on 8 devices: a sensor fault, not a real temperature.

readme-32.claim: Enclosure temperature and humidity come from a 'heater / environment' service, which implies a heater on these devices. Heater power and heater state are not exported, and the sensor's placement is undocumented. Any edge from heater operation to input power is therefore unobservable here.
readme-32.quote: Temperature from the heater / environment sensor. *Source: `sqlite:heaterenv`.*
readme-32.section: Temperatures table, row device_temperature; Sensors table, row device_humidity

readme-33.claim: The light sensor gives ambient light only. The README documents no link between it and display brightness or power, so a light_lux -> input_power edge (auto-dimming) cannot be supported from this source.
readme-33.section: Sensors and activity table, row device_lightsensor

readme-34.claim: The PIR count is a resetting counter that features.py turns into detections per hour. The README documents no effect of detections on display or power.
readme-34.quote: Number of detections by the PIR (passive infrared) motion sensor. *Source: `sqlite:pir`.*
readme-34.section: Sensors and activity table, row device_pir_count

readme-35.claim: WWAN rx/tx are typed as gauges but read as daily-resetting running totals, so features.py treats them as counters and wwan_*_rate is GB per hour. The values come from sqlite:heartbeat, and no modem power figure is given.
readme-35.quote: Data received over the cellular (WWAN) modem. *Source: `sqlite:heartbeat`.* **Note:** Typed as a gauge, but behaves like a running total that restarts about once a day (see Notes on the data).
readme-35.section: Connectivity table, rows device_wwan_rx_gb / device_wwan_tx_gb; features.py COUNTERS

readme-36.claim: deepstream_running is a pgrep process check, and its hourly mean is the fraction of samples in which the process was found. It says the process exists, not how hard the GPU works; any edge to cpu_gpu_power needs NVIDIA documentation.
readme-36.quote: 1 when the DeepStream video-analytics application process is running. *Source: `proc:pgrep`.*

readme-37.claim: ds_error_rate is the hourly increase of a count of DeepStream consumer errors parsed from a log; it is a software-health signal with no documented power relation.
readme-37.quote: Number of DeepStream consumer errors found in the DeepStream log. *Source: `log:deepstream`.*

readme-38.claim: wifi_hotspot_running checks whether a systemd service is active, not whether the radio is transmitting or drawing power; its hourly mean is the fraction of samples active.
readme-38.quote: 1 when the Wi-Fi hotspot service is active (checked with systemd), 0 otherwise. Usually 0. *Source: `cmd:systemctl`.*

readme-39.claim: Total and free RAM both come from sqlite:heartbeat, so mem_used_gb = total - free is a linear definition that survives hourly averaging exactly when both are averaged over the same samples. features.py does not build mem_used_gb itself.
readme-39.section: Compute and storage table, rows device_memory_free_gb / device_memory_total_gb

readme-40.claim: features.py derives hour-of-day and day-of-week from the UTC bucket time (the README says all times are UTC), not local time. The README reads the 05:00 UTC counter resets as local midnight (about UTC-5). A time_of_day context node in local time needs a per-agency time-zone conversion, which neither file documents.
readme-40.relation: time_of_day in features.py = UTC hour (not local)
readme-40.doc_title: analysis/features.py: hourly feature builder (project code, not documentation)

readme-41.claim: Hourly buckets are aligned to UTC epoch hours using the device's own timestamps. For gauges, samples from all scrape targets of a device are pooled into one mean; for counters, the per-target increases are combined with max, because two targets report the same total.
readme-41.quote: # is the increase. Two targets of one device report the same total, so combine them with max.
readme-41.doc_title: analysis/features.py: hourly feature builder (project code, not documentation)

physics-1.claim: Steady-state die temperature is usually written as local ambient temperature plus dissipated power times a junction-to-ambient thermal resistance. So CPU+GPU power heats the CPU and GPU temperature sensors above the air around the module.
physics-1.relation: cpu_gpu_power_watts heats cpu_temp_celsius and gpu_temp_celsius: T = T_local_ambient + R_eff x P (physical). enclosure_temperature stands in for T_A only if that sensor measures the air around the module (inferred).
physics-1.quote: The equation usually assumed to be valid for calculating junction temperature from RθJA is: TJ = TA + RθJA × Power (1)
physics-1.doc_title: Semiconductor and IC Package Thermal Metrics (TI SPRA953D)
physics-1.section: 1.1 Usage, Equation 1 (the PDF glyphs 'R qJA ´' are rendered as 'RθJA ×')

physics-2.claim: A datasheet thermal resistance cannot supply the power-to-temperature coefficient, because the effective resistance depends on the board and the installation. The edge's form is documented, but its coefficient must be fitted for each device or hardware class.
physics-2.relation: The coefficient of cpu_gpu_power_watts -> cpu_temp_celsius / gpu_temp_celsius is system-specific and must be fitted, not taken from a datasheet.
physics-2.quote: Because a system board rarely approximates the test coupon used to determine RθJA, application of RθJA using Equation 1 results in extremely erroneous values.
physics-2.doc_title: Semiconductor and IC Package Thermal Metrics (TI SPRA953D)

physics-3.claim: Tj = TA + RθJA(eff) x P holds only while the power of surrounding components stays constant. Heat from the rest of the module (memory, regulators and so on) also raises the CPU/GPU die temperature, so total module power is a candidate thermal parent alongside CPU+GPU power.
physics-3.relation: orin_power_watts (including its non-CPU/GPU part) heats cpu_temp_celsius and gpu_temp_celsius (physical).
physics-3.quote: If RθJA(effective) can be estimated from thermal modeling or measurements in the system, it is possible to use Equation 1 to calculate the junction temperature assuming the power of the surrounding components on the system does not change.
physics-3.doc_title: Semiconductor and IC Package Thermal Metrics (TI SPRA953D)

physics-4.claim: Most of a chip's heat leaves through the printed circuit board rather than the package surface. Dissipation on a board therefore warms other components on it, and the INA238 die (board_temp_celsius) would be heated by nearby module or converter dissipation only if it shares that board or heat path. Its placement is not documented.
physics-4.relation: orin_power_watts and converter losses (part of input_power_watts) heat board_temp_celsius (physical; holds only if they share a board).
physics-4.quote: In fact, in still-air JEDEC-defined RθJA measurements, almost 70%–95% of the power generated by the chip is dissipated from the test board, not from the surfaces of the package.
physics-4.doc_title: Semiconductor and IC Package Thermal Metrics (TI SPRA953D)

physics-5.claim: Thermal resistance is not constant. It falls as dissipated power rises (2-3x higher at very low power) and is 10-20% lower at 100 C ambient than at 0 C, so the power-to-temperature relation is mildly nonlinear.
physics-5.relation: cpu_temp_celsius = f(enclosure_temperature, cpu_gpu_power_watts) with a nonlinear dependence on power (physical).
physics-5.quote: Therefore, RθJA decreases with increasing power dissipation from a package. For very low power dissipation which results in minimal increase in surface temperature, RθJA is sometimes found to be 2×–3x higher than at rated package power levels.
physics-5.doc_title: Semiconductor and IC Package Thermal Metrics (TI SPRA953D)

physics-6.claim: Package-level thermal transients settle within about 0.1-100 s, far shorter than the 1-hour aggregation. Hourly-mean die and IC temperatures can therefore be modelled as a lag-0 function of hourly-mean power. This does not cover slower masses such as a heatsink or the enclosure.
physics-6.relation: power -> die/IC temperature edges at lag 0 (physical)
physics-6.quote: For power packages, transient thermal effects die out within approximately 0.1 to 100 seconds. This time depends on the chip size, the package type, and size. In addition, it is greatly affected by the PCB stack-up and layout.
physics-6.doc_title: Understanding the Theory Behind Transient Thermal Impedance (MPS Article #0085)

physics-7.claim: The heat path die -> package -> PCB -> ambient behaves as a chain of RC cells, each with time constant tau = theta x C. Larger thermal masses (heatsink, enclosure, battery) respond more slowly than the die.
physics-7.relation: none (time-constant structure: tau = theta x C per stage)
physics-7.quote: The electrical analogy for a given application’s thermal behavior (consisting of an active device, package, PCB, and external ambient) is a chain of RC cells, each having a characteristic time constant (τ). τ can be calculated with Equation (5): τ=θxC
physics-7.doc_title: Understanding the Theory Behind Transient Thermal Impedance (MPS Article #0085)

physics-8.claim: For a lumped body the thermal time constant is tau = rho V c / (h A). Massive bodies with high heat capacity, such as a battery or a heavy enclosure, respond slowly. Whether their lag reaches one hour depends on the unknown enclosure and battery construction.
physics-8.relation: none (tau = rho V c / hA sets the lag of enclosure and battery temperatures; a lag-1 edge is justified only if tau is near 1 h)
physics-8.quote: high density, large volume, or high specific heat all tend to increase the time constant, while high heat transfer coefficient and large area will tend to decrease the time constant.
physics-8.doc_title: MIT 16 Unified Thermodynamics notes, 18.3 Transient Heat Transfer (Convective Cooling or Heating)

physics-9.claim: An outdoor-enclosure designer reports a thermal time constant of about 15 minutes for his own (unspecified) units. If similar for the signs, this is under one hour and supports lag-0 edges into enclosure temperature at hourly resolution. The figure is anecdotal.
physics-9.relation: enclosure thermal lag is under 1 h (supports lag 0; anecdotal)
physics-9.quote: my units have a thermal time constant of around 15 minutes.
physics-9.doc_title: Outdoor Enclosure Temperature Profile Math (M. Biegert, Math Encounters blog)

physics-10.claim: A practitioner's enclosure model treats the solar-driven rise of internal temperature as proportional to insolation (19 C above outside air at maximum insolation), added to the outside air temperature.
physics-10.relation: enclosure_temperature ~= T_outside_air + k x solar irradiance (physical; light_lux is only a proxy for irradiance)
physics-10.quote: Assume that the solar load-based temperature rise is proportional to the level of solar insolation. At maximum solar insolation, we will assume the effective ambient temperature is 19 °C above the actual air ambient temperature.
physics-10.doc_title: Outdoor Enclosure Temperature Profile Math (M. Biegert, Math Encounters blog)

physics-11.claim: Converter loss is input power minus output power, P_DISS = P_IN - P_OUT = (1/eta - 1) x P_OUT, and that dissipation sets the converter's temperature rise above ambient. Power at the sign's input therefore contains every downstream load plus all conversion losses, and those losses become heat inside the enclosure.
physics-11.relation: containment: input_power_watts = sum of downstream loads / eta, so input_power_watts >= orin_power_watts; the difference includes conversion loss (heat), display, modem and heater (inferred)
physics-11.quote: PDISS = module power dissipation = PIN – POUT = (1/η – 1) • POUT ... TA MAX = TBMAX – θBA • PDISS = TBMAX – θBA • (1/η – 1) • POUT
physics-11.doc_title: Vicor Design Guide & Applications Manual, 6. Thermal Performance Information
physics-11.section: Nomenclature and basis of derating curves (p.1)

physics-12.claim: A converter dissipates P_OUT/eta - P_OUT as heat, and its temperature rise over ambient is P_diss x theta. Applied to the solar charge controller, more charge or load power means more loss and a higher controller temperature.
physics-12.relation: mppt_charge_power (and mppt_load_power) heat mppt_controller_temperature through a (1/eta - 1) x P loss (physical)
physics-12.quote: the power dissipated (Pdiss) as heat is: Pdiss = POUT/η – POUT (2) Therefore Pdiss = 61.8W. Now we must determine the baseplate temperature rise over ambient caused by this power dissipation.
physics-12.doc_title: Vicor AN:106 Thermal Considerations: Assuring Performance of Vicor's Maxi, Mini, Micro Series

physics-13.claim: Buck-converter switching loss is proportional to input voltage x output current x switching frequency. For the same downstream load, conversion loss and hence input power depend on the supply voltage.
physics-13.relation: input_power_watts = P_load + a x V_in x I_load + ... (physical); supply_56v and input_voltage_volts modulate the loss
physics-13.quote: PSW-TURN ON = 1/2 × VIN × IOUT × ΔTON × fSW ... Important to note is that the switching losses are linearly proportional with the switching frequency and with the output current.
physics-13.doc_title: Improving Efficiency at Higher Loads with High Switching Frequencies (TI SLUAAA5)
physics-13.section: 2 Main Sources of Power Losses, Switching Losses, Eq. 1

physics-14.claim: Converter conduction loss grows with the square of current. Input power therefore rises slightly faster than linearly with downstream load.
physics-14.relation: input_power_watts = P_load + b x I^2 + ... (nonlinear containment)
physics-14.quote: What is important to notice from these equations is that the conduction losses are dependent on the square of the RMS value of the current flowing through the particular MOSFET and through the inductor.
physics-14.doc_title: Improving Efficiency at Higher Loads with High Switching Frequencies (TI SLUAAA5)
physics-14.section: 2 Main Sources of Power Losses, Conduction Losses

physics-15.claim: As converter input voltage rises with fixed output, the duty cycle falls, switching loss rises and high-side conduction loss falls, while low-side MOSFET and inductor losses rise. The loss mix therefore depends on input voltage.
physics-15.relation: supply_56v / input_voltage_volts -> input_power_watts through converter efficiency (physical)
physics-15.quote: The VIN increases, then duty cycle decreases, the switching loss increases and conduction loss decreases. So the HS MOSFETS is in a trade-off between switching loss and conduction loss. The VIN increases, both the LS MOSFET and the inductor losses increase.
physics-15.doc_title: An Accurate Approach for Calculating the Efficiency of a Synchronous Buck Converter Using the MOSFET Plateau Voltage (TI SLVAEQ9)
physics-15.section: 4 Power Losses Calculation and Efficiency Estimation

physics-16.claim: Against a strong effect: in TI's measured example (5.9 V out, 10 A), efficiency was 94.0% at 6.5 V in and 93.5% at 35 V in. Input voltage shifted efficiency by well under one point, so the supply-voltage effect on input power may be small. The example load is much heavier than a ~10 W sign, and light-load behaviour may differ.
physics-16.relation: against: supply_56v -> input_power_watts via efficiency may be a small effect
physics-16.quote: VIN = 6.5 V, the efficiency of calculated is 94.2%, the test efficiency is 94.0%. ... VIN = 35 V, the efficiency of calculated is 93.9%, the test efficiency is 93.5%.
physics-16.doc_title: An Accurate Approach for Calculating the Efficiency of a Synchronous Buck Converter Using the MOSFET Plateau Voltage (TI SLVAEQ9)

physics-17.claim: At light load, losses that do not scale with load current dominate: switching, MOSFET output-capacitance, gate-charge and controller operating losses. Some grow with input voltage (P_IC = V_IN x I_CC; P_COSS proportional to V_IN^2), so a low-power sign's input power has a load-independent offset that can differ between 12 V and 56 V supplies.
physics-17.relation: input_power_watts has an intercept term that grows with input_voltage_volts (physical)
physics-17.quote: At low currents, there is a greater impact from the switching-loss in the MOSFET, the output capacitance loss in the MOSFET, the gate charge loss in the MOSFET, and the operation loss of the IC.
physics-17.doc_title: Efficiency of Buck Converter (ROHM application note 64AN035E)
physics-17.section: p.10, discussion of loss factors; Eqs. 8 and 12

physics-18.claim: A tightly regulated DC-DC converter draws constant power from its input, so for a fixed downstream load the input current varies inversely with input voltage. A battery's IR drop makes voltage depend on current in turn, giving a lag-0 loop between input voltage and current.
physics-18.relation: input_current_amperes = input_power_watts / input_voltage_volts (constant-power load). The reverse effect (current -> voltage via battery or wiring IR drop) closes a lag-0 loop and must be a feedback note, not an edge.
physics-18.quote: As I mentioned earlier, the feedback loop of a regulated dc-dc converter acts to set the output power of the converter instantaneously constant, rejecting input voltage variations and hence making the converter input port appear as a constant-power load (CPL).
physics-18.doc_title: The Engineer's Guide To EMI In DC-DC Converters (Part 10): Input Filter Impact On Stability (T. Hegarty, Texas Instruments, How2Power Today)
physics-18.section: Closed-Loop Input Impedance Of A DC-DC Converter

physics-19.claim: Heat from components in a sealed enclosure leaves by natural convection through the panels: Q = A x k x dT, with k = 5.5 W/m2K for sheet steel. Internal dissipation therefore raises enclosure air above outside ambient, so enclosure_temperature is partly caused by the sign's own power and is not purely exogenous.
physics-19.relation: enclosure_temperature - T_outside ~= input_power_watts / (k x A) (physical). This conflicts with enclosure_temperature being a context root; keep as a note.
physics-19.quote: In natural convection, heat loss is dissipated to the outside via the enclosure panels. The prerequisite for this is that the ambient temperature must be lower than the temperature inside the enclosure. ... QS = A k ΔT (watts)
physics-19.doc_title: Rittal Technical System Catalogue Climate Control, page 6: Calculation basis for enclosure climate control
physics-19.section: Calculation basis for enclosure climate control (k = 5.5 W/m2K for sheet steel)

physics-20.claim: In an unventilated outdoor telecom cabinet, peak inside air temperature rose about 4 C per 200 W of internal dissipation. The effect of internal power on enclosure air is real but small per watt, so at ~10 W a sign's own contribution is likely small next to sun and weather. The cabinet is much larger than a sign, so this is indicative only.
physics-20.relation: input_power_watts heats enclosure_temperature (physical, weak per watt)
physics-20.quote: It is found that for thermal power dissipated values between 100 W and 700 W, the maximum air temperature inside the OTC increased by about 4°C every 200 W of increase in the value of the dissipated thermal power.
physics-20.doc_title: Characterization of the thermal performance of an outdoor telecommunication cabinet (Silva et al., Int. J. Energy Prod. & Mgmt. 2(1) 106-117)

physics-21.claim: Sun exposure raises the cabinet's inside air temperature during the day, and the surface's radiative properties set how large the rise is.
physics-21.relation: solar irradiance (light_lux as proxy) heats enclosure_temperature (physical)
physics-21.quote: The results show that the OTC radiant properties affect the air temperature during diurnal periods when the cabinet is exposed to solar radiation, with higher air temperature values to higher surface emissivity values.
physics-21.doc_title: Characterization of the thermal performance of an outdoor telecommunication cabinet (Silva et al., Int. J. Energy Prod. & Mgmt. 2(1) 106-117)

physics-22.claim: For a 300x300x400 mm sealed enclosure holding 100 W of electronics, solar load was 0-200 W depending on surface absorptivity, the same order as the internal load. For a ~10 W sign, sunlight is likely the dominant heat input to the enclosure.
physics-22.relation: solar irradiance (light_lux as proxy) heats enclosure_temperature and can match or exceed input_power_watts as a heat source (physical)
physics-22.quote: This works out to a total solar load of anywhere between 0 and 200W depending upon the solar absorptivity of the outer surface. This shows that the solar load can be of the same magnitude as the internal thermal load.
physics-22.doc_title: Evaluation of Cooling Solutions for Outdoor Electronics (Wankhede, Khaire, Goswami, Mahajan; THERMINIC 2007)

physics-23.claim: Solar load is one third to two thirds of an outdoor enclosure's total cooling load.
physics-23.relation: solar irradiance heats enclosure_temperature comparably to or more than internal power (physical)
physics-23.quote: Solar load must be considered in any outdoor application. Solar loads can account from 1/3 to 2/3 of the total cooling load of an outdoor enclosure.
physics-23.doc_title: Thermal management of outdoor enclosures using phase change materials (M. Marongiu, Electronics Cooling)

physics-24.claim: Solar heat input to each enclosure face is insolation x surface absorptivity x area, linear in irradiance, with 1120 W/m2 as the ETSI design value. If light_lux is roughly proportional to irradiance, it is roughly proportional to solar heat input, apart from orientation and placement effects.
physics-24.relation: solar heat input = irradiance x absorptivity x area; light_lux -> enclosure_temperature is a proxy relation (physical)
physics-24.quote: Each heat source is equal to the solar insolation value multiplied by the solar absorptivity of the surface and its area. The model used a solar insolation of 1120 W/m 2 , the value prescribed by the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) [6].
physics-24.doc_title: Characterization of Realistic Environmental Conditions for Predicting the Reliability of Outdoor Cellular Electronics (F. Hawley, Electronics Cooling)

physics-25.claim: Solar radiation peaks about three hours before outdoor air temperature. Light level and air temperature are distinct drivers with different daily phases, so a lux reading cannot stand in for outside air temperature.
physics-25.relation: none between light_lux and outside air temperature beyond the shared time_of_day; the solar peak leads the air-temperature peak by ~3 h
physics-25.quote: Maximum solar radiation occurs approximately three hours before the occurrence of maximum ambient temperature.
physics-25.doc_title: Characterization of Realistic Environmental Conditions for Predicting the Reliability of Outdoor Cellular Electronics (F. Hawley, Electronics Cooling)

physics-26.claim: In a 230 W outdoor radio unit, maximum solar load raised board temperature by 3.0 C. The rise averaged about half that during the day and was zero at night, so sunlight adds a daytime-only, insolation-dependent component to board temperature.
physics-26.relation: solar irradiance (light_lux) heats board_temp_celsius and enclosure_temperature; zero at night (physical)
physics-26.quote: the board temperature rise due to maximum solar load is 3.0 o C. The average solar rise during the day is approximately one-half this value, while the solar rise at night is zero.
physics-26.doc_title: Characterization of Realistic Environmental Conditions for Predicting the Reliability of Outdoor Cellular Electronics (F. Hawley, Electronics Cooling)

physics-27.claim: In a naturally cooled outdoor unit, the internal air above each circuit board was about equal to the average board temperature. Board-mounted temperature sensors and an internal air sensor can therefore track one shared thermal state.
physics-27.relation: redundancy-like: board_temp_celsius tracks enclosure air temperature (shared cause), if both are inside the same compartment
physics-27.quote: Circuit boards and electronic devices are mounted onto heat sinks, which cool the electronics by natural convection. The internal air temperature above each circuit board is approximately equal to the average board temperature.
physics-27.doc_title: Characterization of Realistic Environmental Conditions for Predicting the Reliability of Outdoor Cellular Electronics (F. Hawley, Electronics Cooling)

physics-28.claim: For natural sunlight, illuminance is roughly proportional to solar irradiance (about 120,000 lx at 1000 W/m2). Published conversion factors range widely (21-131 lm/W) with spectrum, so lux is only an approximate irradiance proxy.
physics-28.relation: light_lux ~= 120 x solar irradiance (W/m2) for sunlight (approximate proxy)
physics-28.quote: Peer-reviewed literature contains Luminous Efficacy equivalents values of 21 to 131 lumens per watt. ... Solar Irradiance of 1 Sun (1,000 W/m2) equals approximately 120,000 Lux.
physics-28.doc_title: A Conversion Guide: Solar Irradiance and Lux Illuminance (P. Michael et al., IEEE DataPort; paper in J. Measurements in Engineering 2020)

physics-29.claim: Against lux as a clean proxy: a typical ambient-light sensor can saturate in strong sunlight unless its gain is low, and uncorrected linearity is documented only up to about 1 klx. The sign's lux value may clip or be nonlinear in direct sun; the signs' sensor model is unknown.
physics-29.relation: against: light_lux may saturate or be nonlinear at high irradiance
physics-29.quote: For unknown brightness conditions, the application should always start with the lowest gain: 1/8 or 1/4. This avoids possible overload / saturation if, for example, strong sunlight suddenly reaches the sensor.
physics-29.doc_title: Designing the VEML7700 Into an Application (Vishay application note 84323)
physics-29.section: Application-dependent lux calculation (see also: linear behaviour 'to about 1 klx')

physics-30.claim: A tinted cover glass passes only 1-10% of ambient light to the sensor. The lux scale relative to true outdoor illuminance depends on the sign's window, which is unknown.
physics-30.relation: none (scale factor of light_lux depends on cover glass; affects the coefficients of any proxy edge)
physics-30.quote: If the application uses a darkened / tinted cover glass, just 10 % - or even just 1 % - of the ambient light will reach the sensor.
physics-30.doc_title: Designing the VEML7700 Into an Application (Vishay application note 84323)

physics-31.claim: Solar-cell short-circuit current is linear in light intensity, so panel current and an ambient-light reading share one cause, sunlight. Panel orientation, shading and the MPPT operating point make this only an approximate redundancy; at night both are near zero.
physics-31.relation: redundancy: light_lux ~ mppt_solar_current (shared cause: irradiance); direction by convention
physics-31.quote: The short-circuit current from a solar cell depends linearly on light intensity
physics-31.doc_title: PVEducation: Effect of Light Intensity (Honsberg & Bowden)

physics-32.claim: Ambient-light sensors are commonly used to dim display backlights. If the sign's display brightness follows its light sensor, light_lux would drive input power through display power, which is not measured. BusPas must confirm.
physics-32.relation: possible control: light_lux -> input_power_watts via display backlight (unconfirmed)
physics-32.quote: Ambient light sensor for control of display backlight dimming in LCD displays
physics-32.doc_title: Vishay TEMT6000X01 ambient light sensor product page

physics-33.claim: Battery SOC maps to open-circuit voltage, and under load the terminal voltage differs from OCV by an IR drop. That drop depends on internal impedance, current and battery temperature.
physics-33.relation: mppt_battery_voltage = OCV(mppt_battery_soc_pct, T) +/- I x R(T) (physical). The same applies to input_voltage_volts on battery-fed 12 V signs if the input sits on the battery (wiring unknown).
physics-33.quote: Voltage + IR Correction expands on voltage correlation by taking into account the IR drop that occurs when a load is applied to a battery. The amount of IR drop depends on the internal impedance of the battery, the amount of load current, and the temperature of the battery.

physics-34.claim: TI's CEDV gauge models cell voltage as a function of SOC, temperature and current, using OCV(SoC, T) and resistance R(SoC, T).
physics-34.quote: CEDV algorithm mathematically models cell voltage as a function of the battery’s SOC, temperature, and current.

physics-35.claim: Battery charge is its starting charge plus the time integral of current, so SOC's hour-to-hour change follows that hour's mean net battery current divided by capacity. This is a differenced/lag relation, and an identity if either SOC metric is coulomb-counted (algorithm unknown).
physics-35.relation: mppt_battery_soc_pct(t) - mppt_battery_soc_pct(t-1) proportional to net battery current(t) x 1 h / capacity (identity if coulomb-counted; lag 1)
physics-35.quote: Coulomb counting is a direct measurement of how much electrical charge is leaving or entering the battery. Equation 1 is used for coulomb counting, where the current amount of charge is equal to the starting amount of charge plus the integration of current over time.

physics-36.claim: Usable capacity falls sharply in the cold (TI example: 2250 mAh at room temperature vs ~1100 mAh cold) because of larger IR drop. Battery temperature therefore modulates the SOC-voltage relation and the accuracy of SOC estimates.
physics-36.relation: mppt_battery_temperature modulates the SOC -> voltage relation and the reported SOC (physical)
physics-36.quote: Then if the battery is used in very cold conditions, the total usable capacity could reduce to 1100 mAh, just based on the effects that cold temperature will cause a greater IR drop in the open circuit voltage.

physics-37.claim: After current stops, Li-ion cell voltage takes about 1 hour (DOD 0-80%) to 3-4 hours (DOD above 80%) to relax to OCV, longer when cold. Battery voltage in a given hour therefore depends on current in earlier hours, which supports lag-1 edges from battery current to battery voltage.
physics-37.quote: A well-relaxed state is detected if dV/dt < 4 µV/s or maximal waiting time of 5 hours is exceeded. The first condition is satisfied in typical batteries after about 1 hour if DOD is between 0% and 80%, and 3–4 hours if DOD is above 80%. At a low temperature, relaxation takes a longer time.
physics-37.doc_title: Theory and Implementation of Impedance Track Battery Fuel-Gauging Algorithm in bq20zxx Product Family (TI SLUA364B)
physics-37.section: Timing of DOD0 and Qmax updates during relaxation mode

physics-38.claim: Against a strong SOC -> voltage edge: LiFePO4 cells have an extremely flat OCV-vs-SOC profile and need hours of rest for a valid OCV. If the sign batteries are LiFePO4, SOC tells little about voltage over the mid-range.
physics-38.relation: against: SOC -> battery voltage is weak for LiFePO4 in mid-range SOC
physics-38.quote: This becomes more difficult with the extremely flat voltage profile of lithium-iron-phosphate (LiFePO4 ) cells (see Figure 1), especially if it is not possible to fully discharge the battery and let it rest for several hours.
physics-38.doc_title: Fine-tuning TI's Impedance Track battery fuel gauge with LiFePO4 cells in shallow-discharge applications (K. Keller, TI Analog Applications Journal SLYT402)
physics-38.section: Introduction (p.1); also 'LiFePO4 cells have a very long relaxation time' (OCV Wait Time 5 h)

physics-39.claim: For a 12 V AGM lead-acid battery at 25 C after at least 4 h rest, OCV rises monotonically with SOC: >=12.8 V at 100%, 12.5 V at 75%, 12.2 V at 50%, 11.9 V at 25%, <=11.6 V at 0%. The whole 0-100% range spans only about 1.2 V.
physics-39.relation: OCV ~= 11.6 V + 1.2 V x SOC for a 12 V AGM battery at rest (physical; chemistry of the sign batteries unknown)
physics-39.quote: State of Charge (%) OCV per cell OCV per 12V battery 100 2.13 or greater 12.8 or greater 75 2.08 12.5 50 2.03 12.2 25 1.98 11.9 0 1.93 or less 11.6 or less
physics-39.doc_title: Technical Manual for Lifeline Batteries (Concorde Battery Corp., Document 6-0101)

physics-40.claim: Lead-acid OCV is defined only after enough rest to reach steady state, normally at least 4 hours. A loaded or recently charged battery's voltage reflects recent current, not only SOC.
physics-40.relation: battery current history (lag >= 1 h) -> battery voltage (physical)
physics-40.quote: The voltage of a battery when it is not delivering or receiving power, and has been at rest long enough to reach a steady state (normally, at least 4 hours).
physics-40.doc_title: Technical Manual for Lifeline Batteries (Concorde Battery Corp., Document 6-0101)

physics-41.claim: Battery internal resistance varies with current, SOC, temperature and age, and causes the terminal-voltage drop under load. A partly discharged cell drops more for the same load.
physics-41.relation: input_current_amperes -> input_voltage_volts (IR drop; physical), with R depending on SOC and temperature. This forms a lag-0 loop with the constant-power load, so use a feedback note.
physics-41.quote: Its value varies with the current, state of charge, temperature, and age. With an extremely heavy load, such as an engine starter, the cell voltage may drop significantly. This voltage drop is due to the internal resistance of the cell.
physics-41.doc_title: Technical Manual for Lifeline Batteries (Concorde Battery Corp., Document 6-0101)

physics-42.claim: Against a strong temperature -> rest-voltage edge: the maker states that a fully charged AGM battery's OCV after 4 h rest is at least 13.0 V regardless of battery temperature. This sits slightly above its own table value of 12.8 V.
physics-42.relation: against: mppt_battery_temperature -> resting battery voltage is weak (the temperature effect is mainly through charging set points and IR drop)
physics-42.quote: The open circuit voltage (after at least 4 hours of rest) will be 2.17 volts per cell or higher (13.0 volts for a 12-volt battery), regardless of the battery temperature.
physics-42.doc_title: Technical Manual for Lifeline Batteries (Concorde Battery Corp., Document 6-0101)
physics-42.section: FAQ: How can I tell if my battery is fully charged?

physics-43.claim: The correct lead-acid charge voltage depends strongly on battery temperature: absorption is 14.30 V at 77 F, 14.72 V at 50 F and 14.04 V at 100 F (Table 5-1). With a temperature-compensating controller, battery voltage during absorption and float becomes a function of battery temperature.
physics-43.relation: mppt_battery_temperature -> mppt_battery_voltage (control, during absorption/float, if compensation is enabled)
physics-43.quote: Charging voltage varies widely depending on the battery’s temperature and there is no single voltage that will work over a wide temperature range. Batteries will fail prematurely if this is attempted.
physics-43.doc_title: Technical Manual for Lifeline Batteries (Concorde Battery Corp., Document 6-0101)
physics-43.section: FAQ (outdoor charge voltage) and Table 5-1 Charging Voltage at Different Temperatures

physics-44.claim: In the absorption stage, battery voltage is held at a set point while charge current tapers until the battery is full. Charge current then depends on SOC, and voltage is clamped rather than following SOC.
physics-44.relation: control: mppt_battery_soc_pct -> mppt_battery_charge_current (taper in absorption); mppt_battery_voltage clamped at the set point
physics-44.quote: In the second stage, the voltage is held constant at the same pre-set limit until the charging current tapers to a very low value, at which point the battery is fully charged.
physics-44.doc_title: Technical Manual for Lifeline Batteries (Concorde Battery Corp., Document 6-0101)

physics-45.claim: A lead-acid battery is at about 80-85% SOC when the charger reaches its voltage set point and current starts to taper, which marks the start of absorption.
physics-45.relation: control: absorption begins at ~80-85% SOC; above it, mppt_battery_charge_current falls with SOC at constant mppt_battery_voltage
physics-45.quote: A lead-acid battery is said to be at 80% to 85% SOC (State of Charge) when the voltage set point is met and the current starts to taper; considered the start of absorption.
physics-45.doc_title: Deka (East Penn) Renewable Energy Technical Manual

physics-46.claim: In the bulk stage, charge current is constant, set by what the source can supply, and battery voltage rises as charge is replenished.
physics-46.relation: physical/control: in bulk, mppt_battery_charge_current is limited by available solar power (mppt_charge_power) and mppt_battery_voltage rises with SOC
physics-46.quote: The battery voltage rises because the charging current that is provided by the battery charger is replenishing its internal charge capacity. The charger current is flat (constant) and the battery voltage is rising.
physics-46.doc_title: Deka (East Penn) Renewable Energy Technical Manual

physics-47.claim: The current available to charge the battery is what remains after connected loads are supplied. Net battery current equals charger output minus load current, but whether the reported battery charge current is net or gross is not documented.
physics-47.relation: containment: net battery current = charger output current - mppt_load_current (definition of mppt_battery_charge_current unknown)
physics-47.quote: Available power (current) to the batteries is the remaining power (current) after connected loads are satisfied.
physics-47.doc_title: Deka (East Penn) Renewable Energy Technical Manual

physics-48.claim: Direct sunlight and nearby heat sources raise battery temperature, so battery temperature depends on battery placement relative to the sun and to the electronics.
physics-48.relation: solar exposure (light_lux as proxy) and enclosure heat warm mppt_battery_temperature (physical; battery location unknown)
physics-48.quote: Do not install batteries near heat sources or in direct sunlight that may artificially elevate their temperature.
physics-48.doc_title: Technical Manual for Lifeline Batteries (Concorde Battery Corp., Document 6-0101)

physics-49.claim: Silicon leakage current, and so static power, rises exponentially with junction temperature. This is documented by AMD for its devices and is a generic CMOS effect, not Orin-specific. It creates a power -> temperature -> power feedback; with power -> temperature drawn at lag 0, the reverse must be a feedback note.
